1. INTRODUCTION
The Branch and Bound (B&B) algorithm is a foundational
technique in exact combinatorial optimization, widely used
for solving NP-hard problems Morrison et al. (2016).
B&B operates by systematically enumerating all possible
solutions to the problem in a search tree structure. Each
node in the tree represents a partial solution, and branches
correspond to further decisions or sub-problems derived
from the current partial solution. At each node, bounds are
calculated to estimate the best possible solution that can
be obtained from that branch. If the bound for a branch is
worse than the current best known solution, the branch is
pruned, meaning it is not explored further. This approach
ensures that only promising branches of the search tree are
examined, significantly reducing the number of solutions
evaluated. Consequently, efforts to enhance the efficiency
of B&B have focused on optimizing core components, such
as search strategy, branching strategy and pruning criteria
(Morrison et al. (2016)).
Recent advances in ML have shown promise in augmenting
B&B by guiding key decision points within the algorithm.
For example, ML models have been used to improve
search strategies by learning which sub-problems are likely
to contain optimal or near-optimal solutions, effectively
reducing the search space (He et al. (2014)). In branching
strategy, ML techniques, including supervised learning and
reinforcement learning, have been leveraged to determine
which branches to explore first based on problem-specific
features and past experience (Lodi and Zarpellon (2017)).
Additionally, ML can aid in pruning by learning tighter
bounds or identifying subproblems that can be eliminated
earlier, thus saving computational resources (Balcan et al.
(2018)). These advances have sparked interest in applying
ML, particularly Reinforcement Learning, to dynamically
enhance various components of the B&B algorithm.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a par-
ticularly suitable approach for dynamic decision-making
within optimization frameworks. Unlike supervised learn-
ing, where models are trained on static data, RL enables
an agent to learn by interacting with an environment
and receiving feedback through rewards, which makes it
well-suited for sequential decision-making tasks (Sutton
and Barto (2018)). In the context of B&B, RL can be
applied to dynamically adjust search directions, prioritize
promising branches, and adaptively refine bounds based
on real-time feedback from the search process. Notably,
Q-learning, a simple model-free RL algorithm, has shown
effectiveness in tasks that involve learning optimal actions
in complex, multi-step environment

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text: The Branch and Bound (B&B) algorithm is a foundational technique in exact combinatorial optimization, widely used for solving NP-hard problems Morrison et al. (2016). B&B operates by systematically enumerating all possible solutions to the problem in a search tree structure. Each node in the tree represents a partial solution, and branches correspond to further decisions or sub-problems derived from the current partial solution. At each node, bounds are calculated to estimate the best possible solution that can be obtained from that branch. If the bound for a branch is worse than the current best known solution, the branch is pruned, meaning it is not explored further. This approach ensures that only promising branches of the search tree are examined, significantly reducing the number of solutions evaluated. Consequently, efforts to enhance the efficiency of B&B have focused on optimizing core components, such as search strategy, branching strategy and pruning criteria (Morrison et al. (2016)). Recent advances in ML have shown promise in augmenting B&B by guiding key decision points within the algorithm. For example, ML models have been used to improve search strategies by learning which sub-problems are likely to contain optimal or near-optimal solutions, effectively reducing the search space (He et al. (2014)). In branching strategy, ML techniques, including supervised learning and reinforcement learning, have been leveraged to determine which branches to explore first based on problem-specific features and past experience (Lodi and Zarpellon (2017)). Additionally, ML can aid in pruning by learning tighter bounds or identifying subproblems that can be eliminated earlier, thus saving computational resources (Balcan et al. (2018)). These advances have sparked interest in applying ML, particularly Reinforcement Learning, to dynamically enhance various components of the B&B algorithm. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a par- ticularly suitable approach for dynamic decision-making within optimization frameworks. Unlike supervised learn- ing, where models are trained on static data, RL enables an agent to learn by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback through rewards, which makes it well-suited for sequential decision-making tasks (Sutton and Barto (2018)). In the context of B&B, RL can be applied to dynamically adjust search directions, prioritize promising branches, and adaptively refine bounds based on real-time feedback from the search process. Notably, Q-learning, a simple model-free RL algorithm, has shown effectiveness in tasks that involve learning optimal actions in complex, multi-step environments (Watkins and Dayan (1992)). This makes Q-learning a compelling candidate to start with for enhancing B&B in applications where computational efficiency and solution quality are both critical. One such application is the Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP), a classic NP-hard optimization problem where a set of jobs, each consisting of a sequence of operations, must be scheduled on specific machines to optimize a performance criterion, typically the makespan (total com- pletion time of all jobs) (Michael (1995)). sections.heading: Abstract:
sections.text: The integration of machine learning (ML), particularly reinforcement learning (RL), techniques with classical optimization methods has shown significant potential in addressing the computational challenges of complex combinatorial problems. This paper presents a novel approach that enhances the Branch and Bound (B&B) algorithm with Q-learning, a type of model-free RL, applied to the Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP). While B&B is a powerful method for finding optimal solutions, its computational demands are often prohibitive for large instances. By incorporating Q-learning into the B&B framework (BBQL), the proposed method learns to prioritize promising branches, thereby improving search efficiency and reducing computational overhead. We evaluate BBQL against the classic B&B algorithm on standard JSSP benchmarks. Experimental results indicate that BBQL achieves better makespan results with significantly lower computational costs, highlighting the potential of reinforcement learning to enhance traditional optimization frameworks in scheduling applications. This research offers insights into how AI-driven guidance can improve exact optimization methods, providing a scalable solution to complex scheduling challenges. ∗ Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP G-SCOP, 38000 Grenoble, France (e-mail: ayoub.ouhadi@grenoble-inp.fr, zakaria.yahouni@grenoble-inp.fr, maria.di-mascolo@grenoble-inp.fr).

By incorporating Q-learning into the B&B framework, we aim to create an adaptive approach, termed BBQL (Branch and Bound with Q-Learning), that can leverage learned search strategy to reduce computational demands and improve solution times for JSSP. This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 provides an overview of related work in B&B and ML for scheduling problems. Section 3 details our proposed BBQL approach, including its B&B foundations and Q-learning integration. Section 4 presents the experimental setup, benchmark comparisons, and results. Finally, Section 5 discusses con- clusions and potential directions for future research.

sections.heading: 2. RELATED WORK
sections.text: Integrating ML with Operations Research (OR) has emerged as a powerful approach to tackling complex op- timization and decision-making problems in dynamic en- vironments (Ouhadi et al. (2024)). This synergy leverages the strengths of both fields, with ML providing predictive and adaptive capabilities while OR offers robust optimiza- tion frameworks. Among ML techniques, RL has become particularly prominent in guiding OR algorithms due to its sequential decision-making abilities, which allow for real- time adaptation in optimization processes. Major integra- tion strategies include using ML to guide OR methods dy- namically, generate or refine initial solutions, and enhance the selection and configuration of algorithmic parameters. In scheduling problems, in particular the JSSP, ML and OR integration has demonstrated significant potential. RL methods have been applied to dynamically adjust deci- sions, guiding scheduling heuristics. For instance, Bram- mer et al. (2022) employed Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), an RL-based approach, to optimize job sequencing in a permutation flow shop scheduling problem. Their RL- generated sequences were further improved through local search methods, demonstrating the benefits of integrating RL and traditional optimization. Other hybrid approaches have incorporated Deep Q- Networks (DQN) to enhance probabilistic models within metaheuristics. For example, Du et al. (2022) applied DQN to refine sampling distributions in an Estimation of Dis- tribution Algorithm (EDA) for a flexible job shop schedul- ing problem, dynamically adjusting to varying scheduling requirements. Similarly, Corsini et al. (2022) integrated neural networks with Tabu Search to evaluate machine permutations in JSSP, illustrating how ML can enhance the quality of solutions obtained by heuristic methods. Another important approach involves the Neural Network to assist B&B for Dynamic Berth Allocation Problems (Korekane et al. (2024)). This method incorporates a neu- ral network in an offline setting to predict promising nodes in a Branch and Bound framework, significantly reducing the computational effort. Our approach differs from this work that uses neural networks to predict promising nodes in an offline setting, as our method utilizes online learning within the B&B search process. Recent studies have further explored integrating RL tech- niques with optimization methods for JSSP. For instance, Yang et al. (2025) proposed a hybrid method combin- ing Q-learning and multi-objective genetic algorithms to solve distributed heterogeneous assembly flexible job shop scheduling problems, demonstrating that RL can signifi- cantly enhance genetic algorithms effectiveness in dynamic scheduling scenarios. Including this work highlights the broader applicability and growing interest in RL-based approaches within the scheduling domain. Building on the advancements in ML-OR integration for scheduling, we propose a novel Q-learning-enhanced Branch and Bound (BBQL) approach particularly for JSSP. This method leverages Q-learning to dynamically prioritize branches within the B&B search process, effec- tively reducing the search space and computational cost. Our approach aims to demonstrate that Q-learning can serve as a dynamic guide within the B&B framework, enhancing its scalability for complex scheduling problems. This contribution advances ML-enhanced OR methodolo- gies in general and for scheduling problem in particular, providing a scalable and effective solution to the compu- tational demands of JSSP.

sections.heading: 3. METHODOLOGY
sections.text: The BBQL approach integrates Q-learning with the B&B algorithm to solve the JSSP efficiently. The methodol- ogy combines the structured enumeration of B&B with the adaptive decision-making capabilities of Q-learning to dynamically prioritize promising branches, as shown in Figure 1. Q-learning is then applied to prioritize the best child nodes, guiding the search toward promising branches that may yield good candidate solutions, allowing for quicker pruning of branches with high lower bounds. In this section, we will describe each component of the BBQL framework in detail, beginning with the problem foundation, followed by the B&B algorithm, and finally the integration of Q-learning. 3.1 The job shop scheduling problem Although the family of scheduling problems is large, this paper focuses on the basic JSSP with the makespan objective function. In the JSSP, we have a set of jobs J = { J 1 , J 2 , . . . , J j } and a set of machines M = { M 1 , M 2 , . . . , M m } . Each job J j consists of a sequence of operations ( O j 1 , O j 2 , . . . , O j,k j ) , where k j is the number of operations for job j . Each operation O jk must be processed on a specific machine for a defined processing time p j,k (non-negative) and must follow a given sequence. The objective is to determine a schedule that assigns start ( S j,k ) and completion times ( C j,k ) for each operation ( O jk ) on the assigned machines while satisfying: • The operations of each job must follow a specified order (Constraint 3). • Each machine can process only one operation at a time (Constraint 6). • Operations on the same machine cannot overlap (Constraints 4, 5). The goal is to minimize the makespan C max , defined as the completion time of the last operation among all jobs. If C j is the completion time of job j , the makespan is C max = max j C j . 562 Ayoub Ouhadi et al. / IFAC PapersOnLine 59-10 (2025) 560–565 The problem can be formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP): Minimize C max (1) C ij = S ij + p ij , ∀ i ∈ J, j ∈ O i (2) S i, next ( i,j ) ≥ C ij , ∀ i ∈ J, j ∈ O i (3) S ij ≥ C kl − H · (1 − x ijkl ) , ∀ i, k ∈ J, j, l ∈ O, i ̸ = k (4) S kl ≥ C ij − H · x ijkl , ∀ i, k ∈ J, j, l ∈ O, i ̸ = k (5) x ijkl + x klij = 1 , ∀ i, k ∈ J, j, l ∈ O, i ̸ = k (6) C max ≥ C ij , ∀ i ∈ J, j ∈ O i (7) Where: • C max : Makespan, the maximum completion time of all jobs. • S ij : Start time of operation j in job i . • C ij : Completion time of operation j in job i . • p ij : Processing time of operation j in job i . • H : A sufficiently large constant (big-M method) to enforce constraints. • x ijkl : Binary variable indicating the precedence of operations: · x ijkl = 1 : Operation ( i, j ) precedes operation ( k, l ) on the same machine. · x ijkl = 0 : Operation ( k, l ) precedes operation ( i, j ) on the same machine. • next ( i, j ) : The operation following operation j in job i . 3.2 Branch and Bound Algorithm for JSSP For JSSP, B&B constructs a search tree where each node represents a partial schedule. The algorithm starts with a node representing an empty schedule. The key components of B&B are: •

sections.text: At each iteration, the algorithm selects a node from the priority queue for expansion. Then we generate child nodes by making decisions about which operation to schedule next. Specifically, for JSSP, we select one of the available operations that can be scheduled on a machine without violating job precedence constraints. If multiple operations are eligible to be scheduled on the same machine, each possibility leads to a separate child node. •

sections.text: For each child node generated, we com- pute a lower bound (LB) on the minimum possible makespan achievable from this partial schedule. sections.heading: Pruning
sections.text: : Eliminating branches that cannot lead to an optimal solution or repeated branches. If the lower bound of a child node exceeds the current best-known makespan, the node is pruned, meaning it is not added to the priority queue for further exploration. A Depth-First Search (DFS) strategy is employed as the base search method. This choice is motivated by the sim- plicity of our lower bound calculation, which encourages exploring deeper in the search tree to find candidate so- lutions more quickly. The algorithm 1 outlines the B&B process. It maintains a stack S to manage nodes: • If a node n represents a better complete schedule, it updates the best-known solution. • For incomplete schedules, it computes a lower bound and only expands nodes that could potentially yield a better solution. • When generating children nodes, only those who have a LB inferior to the best known solution (makespan) are kept in L , then inserted into the stack S . We avoid exploring duplicate partial schedules (nodes) by implementing a memorization scheme. Every generated schedule is stored, and any node representing an already encountered partial schedule is pruned from further con- sideration.

Although more sophisticated ranking mechanisms might further improve performance, our objective here is solely to evaluate the incremental benefit provided by the RL guidance. 3.3 Q-Learning Framework To enhance the B&B algorithm, we integrate Q-Learning, a model-free RL method, to guide the selection of the most promising branches. This integration aims to improve the search process by learning optimal policies for branch prioritization based on the current state of each node. sections.heading: 4. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULTS
sections.text: 4.1 Experimental Setup To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed BBQL frame- work, all algorithms are coded using Python 3 and run on a 64-bit machine with Intel Core i7-13700H CPU at a 2.4 GHz processor and 16 GB RAM. The benchmark instances used for testing were obtained from Fisher and Thompson (1963), Lawrence (1984) and Applegate and Cook (1991), 564 Ayoub Ouhadi et al. / IFAC PapersOnLine 59-10 (2025) 560–565 containing a diverse set of JSSP instances. Regarding the experimental setup, each instance is solved five times using different random seeds. Each run is limited to 5 minutes. The final performance metrics are obtained by averaging the results across these runs, ensuring a fair and robust comparison. Moreover, the Q-learning process is executed in an online manner: for every instance, the Q-table is initialized empty and updated during execution, enabling rapid learning despite the simplicity of the tabular ap- proach. State normalization is performed by computing the ratio of the number of jobs in conflict to the total number of jobs, then discretizing this ratio into a limited number of levels (similar to the approach applied to job progress) to maintain a manageable state space. The Q-Learning component of the BBQL framework was configured with the hyperparameters in Table 1. Table 1. Q-Learning Hyperparameters Parameter Value Learning Rate ( α ) 0.1 Discount Factor ( γ ) 0.8 Exploration Rate ( ϵ ) 1.0 ϵ decay 0.997 ϵ min 0.1 These hyperparameters were selected through a grid search process evaluated on randomly generated JSSP instances of medium dimensions, specifically ranging from 6 × 6 to 10 × 10 . In our experimental setup, an episode is defined as the process of finding a complete solution in the B&B tree. During each episode, the agent interacts with the environment of the B&B by selecting actions based on the node state, leading to the construction of a full schedule. Upon finding a complete solution, the exploration rate ϵ is updated according to the ϵ decay , gradually reducing the probability of random actions and increasing the exploitation of learned policies. This approach ensures that the agent increasingly uses its learned knowledge to prioritize promising branches within the B&B framework as training progresses. After reaching the minimum value of ϵ , the agent is still doing exploration with a value of ϵ min . 4.2 Results and Discussion To evaluate BBQL, we compare it with the classic B&B algorithm first across multiple JSSP instances. The com- parison focused on two primary metrics: the number of nodes explored and the computational time required to achieve solutions within 1% of the best makespan ob- tained by classic B&B. In addition, we compared solu- tion quality with several dispatching rules: SPT (Shortest Processing Time), SRPT (Shortest Remaining Processing Time), LPT (Longest Processing Time), LRPT (Longest Remaining Processing Time), and FIFO (First In, First Out). sections.heading: 5. CONCLUSION AND PERSPECTIVES
sections.text: In this work, we investigated the integration of B&B, a classic operations research technique, with Q-Learning, a reinforcement learning method, for solving the JSSP with the makespan criterion. The resulting framework, BBQL, uses the strengths of both domains. Notably, BBQL em- ploys an online learning approach, where the Q-learning agent learns directly from the interactions with the B&B search process during problem solving. This eliminates the need for any pre-training phase, making the framework more adaptable to different problem instances and set- tings. Q-Learning dynamically learns to prioritize the most promising regions of the solution space, effectively guiding Table 2. Comparison of the computation time required by classic B&B and BBQL to achieve the same solutions under a maximum time limit of 5 minutes. BBQL consistently converges faster across the majority of tested instances. the B&B search. This leads to a significant reduction in the number of explored nodes by 79.68% and an impor- tant decrease in computation time by 74.82% compared to the classic B&B algorithm while maintaining solution quality. BBQL consistently outperformed the classic B&B and various dispatching rules in terms of solution quality, achieving an average error in makespan of 14.11%. While our current study demonstrates the potential of integrating tabular Q-learning with a classical B&B al- gorithm, several avenues remain for further exploration. First, a comparison with a classical MILP approach would provide a comprehensive performance baseline and fur- ther highlight the relative advantages of the RL guidance incorporated in our BBQL framework. Additionally, the limitations of tabular Q-learning become apparent as the problem size increases. Although effective for the small di- mensional state space considered in this study, the tabular approach may not scale well for larger instances. Future work will investigate the use of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques, in which state information is encoded within a neural network. This enhanced representation could incorporate richer features (such as detailed machine metrics or additional operational parameters) to better capture the complexity of larger scale JSSP. Moreover, our current implementation utilizes a DFS strategy within the B&B framework. Future research will explore alternative search tree methods, such as beam search, in combination with advanced Q-learning variants, to evaluate whether these strategies can further improve search efficiency. This research provides a promising foundation for hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of operations re- search and machine learning for solving complex optimiza- tion problems.
